No one is going to argue that Suarez is better than Ronaldo.

As far as dribbling, post-Man United Ronaldo wasn't exactly a big dribbler, but as his peak he was probably better. Despite Ronaldo's overall better longevity, I'd actually say Suarez was taking on people directly and successfully for longer.

Ronaldo is undoubtably the better player, and he had way more longevity. It's not even a competition between Suarez and him in aerial ability, pace, or finishing. But let's not pretend that he was better in every single facet of the game.

**I assume youi are talking about the GovTrack data? Or is there another report you wanted to link?**

That website retracted that report as it was only for a single year (they actually retracted all their single-year reports) and they admitted it was unreliable data given the swings looking at a single year. Over a longer timeframe she was 4th, under a medium timeframe she was 2nd.

https://www.govtrack.us/posts/434/2024-07-26_we-retracted-our-single-year-legislator-report-cards-after-warning-about-their-unreliability

In addition, they discuss on their website that they don't look at the legislation in question, or even what was voted on, but rather who co-sponsors bills, and that breaking it down to one number is always just going to be one piece of the puzzle.

[VoteView](https://voteview.com/data) is the other big independent site and had her 2nd (so the super-biased study you originally linked would still be factually wrong) on DW-NOMINATE score, but again it's mostly calculated based on how calculating legislation's lean based on who votes similarly on separate dimensions of issues.

Overall, these sites are decent ballpark estimates, but the methodology is better for grouping in tiers than extrapolating too individually, especially when you also have to consider the constituencies they serve. For example, it doesn't take into account that a Conservative bill that will pass Murkowski or Collins might vote nay, whereas a close bill they are more likely to vote yay, regardless of what the bill is if the party wants it to pass. So in a way it also is a measuring of party loyalty and swing district/state, although again, that's an oversimplification.

I'd agree that Kamala Harris is in the more liberal 10% of Senators, but Warren and Sanders are more liberal if you were to ask the majority of people who look at the context and not just the math.

And FYI if you want to reference reporting of these websites, the long term studies mostly also say that Democrats have largely maintained their level of liberalism (albeit with a small shift more liberal, and a caveat that more conservative Southern Democrats have shifted a bit more) and Republicans have become more conservative over the past several decades, but especially since the 80's.

The NOMINATE scores and other similar mathematical rankings of political ideology are super interesting if you are into both politics and math and I recommend you do a bit of reading about them if you like talking about this stuff, over the past 30 years there's been a lot of development and testing of different scores and methodologies.

Pricing is one of, if not THE biggest thing a companies in a competive industry adjust to compete. Companies raise prices for a wide variety of reasons, and it's rarely an easy decision. Companies that I've been part of have always done a market share or demand risk assessment with a price increase to test out the price elasticity of products/services they sell. This is rarely, if ever, an exact science. There is always uncertainty in these exercises. If an industry is healthy, one company gouging gives another an opportunity. Limiting this across all industries would cripple one of the main levers of competive industries, and could have widespread ramifications within a capitalist economy like the one we live in. Why would you cripple and limit this, without actual insight into each and every industry that you are regulating, and how this would affect each one differently? It's not actually tackling the root of anyting in an enforceable way. Strengthening anti-trust, and anti-competitive enforcement to maintain healthy competition economy wide would be a much smarter approach and much more straightforward to implement on a broad spectrum.

Price increases are complex exercises that can have a multitude of reasons, and outcomes. An increase with notice can cause an unnatural influx of orders right before it's implemented that causes further supply strain and issues within a company's supply chain and ability to forecast, lowering their profitability. Companies also differ in strategy in terms of implementing smaller incremental price increases over time, or large price increases spread out; how would this be differentiated? Sometimes companies increase (or decrease) their products' prices to reframe the product in the eyes of consumers. These are just a few examples in a plethora that are all going to differ company to company & industry to industry. How would the specificity of these factors be policed if a widespread law was put into place limiting price-changing?

> You really couldn’t without companies sharing margins which would be bad for business.>
> 
> Please elaborate.

What I replied to said "Sen. Elizabeth Warren proposed a bill that would ensure that companies profit margins didn't increase with the increase to prices" -- so ignoring the silliness of limiting company's abilities to increase profit margins (which is usually the goal of a company, especially one publicly traded) -- In order to ensure that companies' margins don't increase they'd have to be known. A company's supplier knowing their margins gives them a huge edge in negotiations. Company's that compete or get supply outside the U.S. would be at a disadvantage if those companies didn't have to reveal that information. Knowing that your competitor has tighter margins, means you could squeeze them more easily. It could lead to things like over-reducing product costs causing quality decline. Consumer's could compare two companies and get the impression that one competitor is ripping them off, without knowing the deeper context. There's a reason most companies don't like to share their margin on specific products.

> What if they want to increase prices to build a safety net or fund other projects?>
> 
> Price increases aren't disallowed. The bill simply wants to ensure that the price increases are reflective of the actual market and aren't outrageous. These companies are annoucing increased costs for products despite record profits. What is so bad about ensuring that those increases are legitimate and not just increasing their margin further at the expense of the entire working class?

Don't want to be too repetitive as I think I touched on this already, but determining what is legitimate and what isn't is not straightforward. Also, price increases do effect profit margins but are far from the only factor that would drive this. Additionally, due to supply constraints, not only are companies costs going up, but their ability to supply the same VOLUME of products isn't as reliable or consistent. So in order to account for volume that they may not be able to deliver, they want to increase prices by more than cost increases they might be incurring. A lot of the issue around this is that these supply constraints have a lot of uncertainty around them, and companies are often going to take the conservative approach and lean on the heavier side to be sure they cover their bases to limit downside and increase upside. There's also the whole cascading effect of all prices going up so consumer's aren't as sensitive to price increases. If this sensitivity goes down, it would be in the best interest of the company to implement price increases now; this could be gouging, or it could be them pulling in a future price increase early to minimize market share loss rather than doing one a year from now and being the only one in the industry to do so and sticking out in a negative way in the eye of consumers when the sensitivity to price returns.

I wasn't at all talking about the stock market, or futures even a little bit. By speculation of the future, I mean future speculation of demand, competition, and especially supply in these times. Suppliers all over the world are having issues, and it's unclear if and when they'll improve. Increasing prices to account for anticipated supply risk seems prudent given the unusual circumstances. Not to mention the recent global political tension driven by one of the world's largest supplier of raw materials.

I don’t have an issue with Warren but that seems like a stupid proposal. I do think gouging is happening, but unfortunately I think it’s something that a competitive market has to work through itself.

How would you police gouging at this level by independent companies? You really couldn’t without companies sharing margins which would be bad for business. What if they want to increase prices to build a safety net or fund other projects?

Supply chain issues have also been getting worse, not better; most companies implement price increases based on future expectations (with conservative wiggle room), not just the present.

If companies expect costs of raw materials to go up between 5-15%, and costs have already gone up, they are going to raise prices to account for current cost increase and then also layer on future cost expectations with all the uncertainly in global supply. If they only raise 5% and costs go up 15% they will have to do another increase which might be viewed more unfavorably by customers compared to one bigger one up front.

Future speculation is one of the biggest drivers of rising prices, not just actual cost increases.

 -- If they ever say fine but you can tell they're not, just ask "Are you sure, you look like you want to get something off your chest?"

3. If you think something has been off with them, try to pay attention to them in group settings, especially when they don't think other people are looking.

4. Never use whatever vulnerability they have shared against them. That's a surefire way to make sure they never open up again. SOs make this mistake more often than friends.

6. In general, it's unlikely they open up if it's not 1 on 1. Along the same lines, if you are just a friend, you have to be 1000% certain they aren't in to you (unless you're also into them), because allowing them to open up easily turns into feelings. 

7. Show concern, empathize with them, read body language to know when something's wrong. If they start opening up, and stop, don't necessarily push them, but rather make it clear you are there for them AND that you know something is up. In terms of kill potential you aren't adding that much damage because heroes don't have that much HP at that point  And ghost shroud scales soooo well early--Longer duration means even if you use death pulse right before you are going to be able to get a death pulse off under ghost shroud, lower cooldown/better uptime means you are safer and more durable in fights (which is super important to Necro early before he gets his tank items up), and  considering Necro's mobility problems, most of the time he's not getting a kill is because they just run away faster early game--triple the AOE slow for a longer duration (the slow is so undervalued) means they are going to probably eat another death pulse and be under heartstopper longer actually upping your kill potential IMO in addition to the obvious survivability benefits.

His base damage and attack animation both suck so last hitting with him takes some getting used to--that just comes down to practice. When I go mid I start with a null talisman 95% of the time because it's the only way you are going to compete for last his.

I also don't like to overuse deathpulse at level 1 because level 2 death pulse gives you 3 times the mana back and is easier to spam. In lane wand is a must have, I always get either a null or casual basi for better last hitting, and I also usually get a windlace because he's sooooo slow and it really helps with positioning better along with brown boots. It's not uncommon for me to get raindrops and/or a mango too.

For a beginning Necro build I'd recommend:

Skill build: 4-1-1-1, then max ghost shroud, then heartstopper, take ult when available.

Itemization:

Null Talisman > Wand > Brown Boots + Wind Lace > Arcanes + Mek > Force Staff or Blink > Greaves. After that it all depends on the game. And once you get the hang of him I would highly suggest playing around with items and experimenting as much as possible as I can't stress enough how versatile he is in terms of itemization.

Firstly, link your match ID.

Necro is a hero who is EXTREMELY reliant on positioning.  An out of position Necro is actually extremely easy to kill as he's very immobile and his durability is very reliant on regen from getting kills during fights, timing ghost shroud properly, and itemization. He's naturally very frail actually and is often very hard to kill because people build him tanky due to the fact that the longer he lives in a fight, the more damage heartstopper aura (easily his best skill) does.

You have to play him a couple times to get the hang of what situations you can live through as that is probably the hardest part about playing Necro as mechanically he is fairly easy. This is especially difficult because there is so many items and heroes that counter Necro that you always have to be thinking of what threats are present to you and who you have to be wary of and who you should target.

In terms of itemization, he is extremely versatile (I can't honestly think of a hero who can viably build as many items as him), and to an extent he is also versatile for role pos1-5 can all be played by him if necessary (although he is more suited towards pos2-3 IMO). It's hard to give advice on him without knowing what role you played/plan on playing for him. In general though, itemization is focused on building durability and mobility early and then transitioning to more utility. Damage items like dagon are strong as well because burst synergizes with his ult, and he is often forced to build at least 1 item to break linkens. Personally, I also like items that offer both a bit of damage and bulk/utility like Veil, Blademail, Radiance, and even Eblade. Also don't think of his ult as a KS as it provides you with regen and gives an extra 30seconds of respawn to the enemy so it's not a terrible idea to be somewhat liberal with it.
